newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks snarled on arms, Sinn Fein. [CORRECTED 12:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks snarled on arms, Sinn Fein. [CORRECTED 12:05 GMT]

text.p: Northern Ireland peace talks began the countdown on Wednesday to a vote on the surrender of guerrilla arms that could decide whether the Irish Republican Army resumes a broken truce.

Pro-British Protestant Unionist parties and the pro-Irish Catholic SDLP group have to vote on Anglo-Irish proposals on "decommissioning" arms by July 23 (Corrects from June 23) to allow the slow-moving talks to move onto key issues when they resume in September.
A new truce by the IRA would pave the way for its political wing, Sinn Fein, to enter the negotiations, from which it is currently barred because of the guerrilla war.
The surrender of arms has dogged negotiations on a political settlement to the Northern Ireland conflict since they began one year ago, and there was little sign of an immediate breakthrough.
Unionist Parties, guardians of the province's British sovereignty, are furious that Britain has resumed contact with Sinn Fein, whose IRA allies have fought British rule for nearly three decades.

They suspect Britain has hatched a deal to persuade the IRA to renew its broken 17-month ceasefire. Britain admitted this week that it had answered calls for "clarification" from Sinn Fein despite having broken off talks with the party after the IRA murdered two policeman in June.

"What we have at the moment is that this revelation of these very substantial contacts with Sinn Fein/IRA is casting a shadow over our negotiations today," Reg Empey, negotiatior for the Ulster Unionist Party, told reporters as the talks began.
"What assurances are being given to Sinn Fein/IRA that we don't know about? I think clarification is one thing -- this has gone far and away beyond clarification."
Unionists fear that Britain is going out of its way to lure Sinn Fein to the conference table to get all parties to iron out a settlement that has eluded successive governments for decades.

Sinn Fein and its IRA backers say they should be represented at the talks like any other political party because of its electoral backing. Party president Gerry Adams and his chief negotiator both won seats to the British parliament in a general election on May 1.

The IRA says it should not be required to hand over a single bullet, let alone its stocks of semtex plastic explosive and automatic weapons, until a final political settlement between pro-British Protestant Loyalists and Irish Catholic nationalists is agreed.
Hardline Unionists led by Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party say that Sinn Fein should not be admitted to the talks at all unless the IRA is disarmed and dismantled.

But under compromise proposals by Britain and Ireland, the sponsors of the negotiations, decommissioning would take place in parallel with the political negotiations to show good faith and build trust between the rival blocs.
Sinn Fein said this week that it needed clarification from Britain about the negotiations. Precise details of what it needs to know have not been made clear.

The Irish News, which is read mainly by Catholics, reported on Tuesday that Sinn Fein had also been in contact with the Irish government of Prime Minister Bertie Ahern and President Bill Clinton's Washington administration.
Clinton called Ahern on Tuesday to congratulate him on his June 6 election victory and discuss Northern Ireland.

"They had a very warm chat," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "They clearly reviewed the current efforts by both the Irish government and by the British government to move the Northern Ireland peace talks into a more substantive phase -- ideally with the participation of Sinn Fein based on an unequivocal ceasefire."
